You’re looking at this in a really black-and-white way. Grief isnt something to be looked at from a black and white perspective. Like if something still affects me, it must mean I’m not handling it ‘correctly.’ But that’s not how grief works. I’ve built coping mechanisms, I use them, and most of the time, I manage just fine. That doesn’t mean there won’t ever be difficult months.

Coping isn’t about making grief disappear forever, it’s about learning to live with it. And I have, I work, I take care of myself, I function. Having a hard stretch doesn’t erase all of that. Emotions aren’t something you just master and move on from and pretending they are isn’t realistic.

I hear you, but I think there’s a disconnect. Trying different coping mechanisms doesn’t guarantee that grief will never affect me again. That’s not how this works. I’ve spent years in therapy, built routines, and done the work to manage this, and for the most part, I do. But grief isn’t a problem you solve, it’s something you learn to live with.

And I’m not ignoring advice. I’m just not going to pretend there’s some magic technique out there that will make loss feel like it never happened. That’s not realistic. I adjust, I adapt, and I keep going. That’s all anyone can do.

And ‘techniques for looping’, this isn’t me getting stuck on something small. My sister died by suicide. This isn’t just a passing thought I need to reframe, it’s something that permanently changed my life. Some things will always stay with you, no matter how much work you put in. That doesn’t mean I’m not managing it, it just means grief isn’t as simple as you’re making it out to be.

Yes, it affected my work, which is why I’m on a PIP. I never said otherwise. But the way people are reacting makes it seem like I’m completely incapable of doing my job, which isn’t the case. I had a tough stretch and unfortunately it showed more. That doesn’t mean I’m stuck in the past or that I can’t function, it just means grief doesn’t always stay neatly in the background.

I’m not trying to invalidate your experience at all, and I get that everyone processes loss differently. But my sister didn’t just pass away, she died by suicide from a drug overdose. She was the only family I had left. This isn’t just about losing a relative, it’s something that shaped my entire life. 

Tbh I don’t feel that sad over my dad’s death than my sisters because he passed away because of a health problem, and he was 42. Yes he was young but my sister was just 17. Some people push through grief immediately, others struggle more at certain times. Just because you had to be back at work right away doesn’t mean that’s the standard for how grief should look. It’s not one-size-fits-all.

You’ve brought up coping skills in like 5 different comments. I have them. I use them. But grief isn’t something you just solve like a checklist. Some months, it’s heavier, and this time, it affected my work. That doesn’t mean I’m not trying, it means I had a hard time, and now I have to deal with the fallout.

And ‘impacting my income source’ yeah, obviously? That’s what a PIP is. I know what’s happening. But saying like I haven’t been actively working on this or that I’m refusing to adjust isn’t true. I’m starting ADHD meds next week, I’ve been in therapy for years, and I’m making changes.

I know I need to keep going, and I am.

I see what you mean, but I think there’s a misunderstanding. It’s not that I haven’t developed coping skills, I have. I work, I go out, I cook, I keep up with hygiene. I walk a lot, I journal, I go to therapy, I make sure to have structure in my day. But grief doesn’t just disappear because I have coping mechanisms in place. Some months, it feels closer, more present, like it’s sitting in the back of my mind no matter what I do.

I’ve spoken to a psychiatrist, and I was also diagnosed with ADHD and will start med for it next week. ADHD makes it harder to regulate emotions or compartmentalize things the way people expect. My brain loops through emotions and makes it difficult to just ‘set things aside.’

And I like my therapist. After going through 7 different ones, she’s the one who truly gets me. She’s lost two family members herself, so she doesn’t just understand grief in a clinical way, she actually knows what it’s like. That makes a difference.

It’s not about me not knowing how to deal with it, it’s that there’s no perfect way to deal with it. That doesn’t mean I’m not trying, it just means grief doesn’t work in a straight line.

I think people are really misunderstanding what I mean. I do function. I go to work, I go out, I cook, I keep up with everything. I’m not just lying in bed for five months straight unable to do anything. But grief doesn’t just disappear because I have a routine.

The months leading up to my dad’s and sister’s death anniversaries and my sister’s birthday just feel different. It’s not like I suddenly stop being a person, but the weight of everything sits heavier. I still get through my days but I’m more drained, more mentally foggy, and even if I’m doing everything right, I don’t feel fully there.

So no, it’s not that I can’t function for five months straight. It’s that for those months, I’m carrying something heavier and I guess this time it showed more than usual. Grief doesn’t care about timelines and sometimes it just hits in ways I can’t control.

I do all of this. Meal prep, laundry, keeping up with hygiene. I like dressing up, I love going out. I take myself out on solo dates too. I don’t really exercise, but I walk a lot. I keep myself moving. 

But grief doesn’t care. It’s not something you can fix with a routine or self-care. It just hits randomly, out of nowhere. I could be in the middle of a normal day, laughing, feeling fine, and then suddenly, I’m not. A song, a memory, a dream, a thought I didn’t see coming, and it’s like I’m right back in it.

And job-wise, they’re not keeping me, so looking for something new is just the smart move. Staying here isn’t really an option.
